nameStory: This microscopic algae doesn't have a common name since it's only visible under a microscope - most people never encounter it directly! The scientific name Staurodesmus comes from Greek words meaning 'cross-shaped bond,' referring to how these tiny cells connect to each other in delicate chains.
description: Staurodesmus extensus is a single-celled freshwater algae that's invisible to the naked eye, measuring only about 20-30 micrometers across. Under a microscope, each cell looks like a tiny green gem with distinctive spines or projections extending outward. These microscopic plants float freely in ponds, lakes, and slow streams, often forming part of the green 'soup' you might notice in still water during warm months.

idTips.label: Cell shape with spines
idTips.description: Under high magnification, cells appear roughly triangular or star-shaped with 2-4 prominent spines extending from the corners

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Extremely small at 20-30 micrometers - about 1/50th the width of a human hair

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: Bright emerald green color from chlorophyll, visible as tiny green specks under microscope

idTips.label: Cell wall appearance
idTips.description: Smooth, glassy-looking cell wall that appears almost crystalline under proper lighting

idTips.label: Swimming behavior
idTips.description: Moves slowly through water with gentle rotation, unlike the jerky movement of some other microscopic algae

habitat: Found in clean, slightly acidic freshwater including mountain ponds, bog pools, and quiet backwaters of streams throughout New England's forests. Prefers cooler water temperatures and is often most abundant in shaded areas or deeper water where temperatures remain stable.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water warms, becoming more numerous in late spring pond samples.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when they contribute to the green tint of pond water.
seasonality.fall: Numbers decline as temperatures drop, though some individuals persist in warmer microhabitats.
seasonality.winter: Present in very low numbers, surviving as dormant cells under ice cover.

funFact: These tiny algae are actually living jewels - their cell walls contain silica (glass) and their geometric shapes are so perfect they were once used to test the quality of microscope lenses!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other spiny desmids like Staurodesmus triangularis, but extensus has longer, more prominent spines and a more elongated overall shape. Remember: extensus = extended spines.
contextualKnowledge: This organism represents an entire invisible world of microscopic plant life that most people never realize exists in every drop of pond water. Desmids like this are considered among the most beautiful microscopic organisms and were favorite subjects of Victorian-era microscopists.
compareHints: Staurodesmus extensus differs from its relatives by having the longest spines in the genus - hence 'extensus' meaning extended. Unlike S. triangularis which is more compact, or S. convergens which has inward-curving spines, extensus has straight spines that project boldly outward from the cell body.
